title: Whittled birch whistle
subtitle: Green-wood whittling: a sounding whistle from a birch branch
excerpt: A simple one-note sounding whistle whittled from a straight birch branch. The pith is pushed out to make the bore, a notch cut for the mouthpiece, and a plug fitted to direct the air. The whole project takes under an hour with a sloyd knife and a round-section rod.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the pith-bore whistle construction; Carpentry for Boys (1914) for the mouthpiece notch geometry.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. The soft pith of a green birch branch can be pushed out cleanly to make the whistle bore.
A short section of branch, used here as the whistle tube.

content.text: A pith-bore whistle is one of the oldest and simplest woodworking projects: a length of young birch branch with the soft pith pushed out to form the air tube, a notch cut to make the sounding edge, and a tapered plug whittled to fit the mouthpiece end. The pitch varies with the length of the tube and the size of the notch, a 15 cm tube produces a low tone; a 10 cm tube a higher one. Spring-cut birch, when the sap is running, gives the cleanest pith removal; autumn-cut birch still works but the pith is firmer.
. Source a young birch branch with a soft, straight pith.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

cut from a young branch 12, 15 mm in diameter, 15 cm long. The pith should be central and straight, hold the section up to a light source and sight along the end-grain to check. Elder or willow also have soft, pushable pith; elder is traditional for folk instruments.
A thin straight stick or 4 mm dowel for pushing out the pith.
Any comfortable seat. The pith-pushing makes a mess; work outdoors or over a tray.

Insert a thin straight stick into one end of the billet and push it through to the other end. The soft pith in fresh birch comes out as a solid plug or as a soft paste, leaving a clean cylindrical bore. If the pith resists, twist the stick as you push. The bore does not need to be perfectly smooth for a working whistle.

to remove the bark from a 3 cm section at one end (the mouthpiece end). Flatten one side of this section until you just expose the bore, a flat ramp about 1 cm long leading from the outside down to the bore opening. This ramp directs the blown air across the sounding notch.
About 3 cm from the mouthpiece end, cut the sounding notch: a rectangular slot, 5 mm long and 3 mm wide, cut through the same flat face you just made. Make a
at each end of the slot first, then remove the waste between them. The far edge of the notch (the sounding edge) should be a clean, sharp right-angle where the flat surface meets the bore.
Step 4: Whittle and fit the plug

From a scrap of the same branch, whittle a tapered plug the same diameter as the bore at the thick end, tapering to slightly less at the thin end. Insert the plug into the mouthpiece end, flat-face up, and push it in until the front face of the plug is flush with the back edge of the sounding notch. The plug should be snug but removable, if it swells and locks in as the wood dries, soak the mouthpiece end in water briefly and twist the plug out.

Blow gently into the mouthpiece. The whistle should sound. If no sound: check the plug is flush with the notch back edge, not protruding past it. If the sound is breathy: the notch sounding edge is not sharp enough, deepen the stop cut slightly. If the sound is too sharp to be pleasant: lengthen the tube by cutting the open end at a slight angle.
No oil finish for a whistle. Leave plain or apply a thin coat of beeswax to the outer surface for weather resistance. Remove the plug before storing to prevent it swelling stuck.
Two-hole whistle: drill or burn two finger holes along the tube with a hot wire to give two additional notes.
Elder whistle: elder wood has an even softer pith than birch and has been used for folk flutes across northern Europe for centuries.

Remove the plug after use and allow the bore to dry. A damp bore over time will stain and decay. If the whistle stops sounding cleanly, the plug has swollen, remove, carve a thin shaving off the plug sides, and refit.

attrs.cause: Plug is either too short (air escaping around the plug) or too long (plug protrudes past the notch and blocks the sounding edge)
attrs.fix: Check the plug is flush with the back edge of the notch. If the plug is too long, trim the front face. If there is a gap between the plug and the bore wall, carve a slightly larger plug.
